title: Olympic hero Alysa Liu to sit out figure skating season before 2027 return
description: Olympic champion Alysa Liu will sit out the 2026-27 figure skating season, taking another break from competition while continuing to train ahead of a planned return the following year.  “I always want to challenge myself in new ways, so my artistry and skating can evolve,” Liu wrote.  Liu told NBC Sports that she intends to continue working with her longtime Bay Area coaches, Phillip DiGuglielmo and Massimo Scali, with an emphasis on her “overall artistry, spins, jumps, everything”.
fullText:
Olympic champion Alysa Liu will sit out the 2026-27 figure skating season, taking another break from competition while continuing to train ahead of a planned return the following year.

The 21-year-old American announced her decision on social media, saying she wanted time to "recalibrate" and develop her skating away from the demands of competition.

"I always want to challenge myself in new ways, so my artistry and skating can evolve," Liu wrote. "It's important to me that my sport reflects my personal growth."

Liu told NBC Sports that she intends to continue working with her longtime Bay Area coaches, Phillip DiGuglielmo and Massimo Scali, with an emphasis on her "overall artistry, spins, jumps, everything".

"I really want to improve my skating, and I wanted to take the time to do that for myself and just to evolve," she said. "And then I'll be back after that is done."

The decision represents another unconventional turn in a career that has carried Liu from child prodigy to burnout, retirement and an unlikely return as world and Olympic champion.

Liu became the youngest ever US women's champion aged 13, when her 4ft 6in frame left her too short to reach the top of the podium without help from the other medalists. But the relentless training and attention that accompanied her rapid ascent gradually drained her enthusiasm for the sport.

She retired at 16, only months after finishing sixth in her Olympic debut at the 2022 Beijing Games, and later described how comprehensively she had come to reject the life built around her skating.

"I really hated skating when I quit," Liu said in the run-up to the Milano Cortina Olympics. "I didn't care about competitions. I didn't care about places. I didn't care about skaters. I didn't care about my programs. I just wanted to get away."

Liu enrolled at UCLA, studied psychology and went hiking in the Himalayas with friends while discovering an identity beyond the rink. Her desire to skate returned unexpectedly during a ski trip to Lake Tahoe, where gliding down the mountain rekindled her love of movement.

She began skating once a week at public sessions in El Segundo, California, and found that the difficult jumps that had propelled her childhood rise had not entirely deserted her. Liu eventually decided to mount a comeback, but only with greater control over her career, including her music, costumes, diet and training schedule.

The results would no longer define the experience, she insisted. Her initial ambition was simply to make another Olympic team and use the sport as a form of self-expression.

That approach carried Liu to a surprise world championship in 2025, making her the first American woman to win the title since Kimmie Meissner in 2006. In February, she landed seven clean triple jumps to rise from third place after the short program and win the Olympic women's singles title in Milan.

The West Oakland native became the first American woman to claim the event since Sarah Hughes in 2002. She also won gold in the Olympic team competition.

"Really the only word that comes to mind when I think about my entire journey is grateful," Liu told NBC Sports. "I think the reason why it's been so fun is because I have my own agency. I really like to skate, and so that's why I skate."

Liu said she assessed her emotional and physical state earlier this summer and concluded that stepping away was the right choice. DiGuglielmo and Scali supported the decision.

"Logically and emotionally and physically, this just makes the most sense," she told NBC Sports. "I will miss seeing the international competitors at all the international competitions, but there will be more, so it's fine."

A rush of opportunities followed Liu's Olympic victory. Nearly 5,000 people turned out for a homecoming celebration in her honor, where Oakland mayor Barbara Lee presented her with a key to the city. She withdrew from the world championships in March, performed alongside her Olympic teammates on the Stars on Ice tour, attended Louis Vuitton's Paris Fashion Week show and wore the label to the Met Gala.

Liu had been scheduled to compete at Skate America from 13-15 November in Everett, Washington.

title: Why does college football generate so many Freezing Cold Takes?
description: Fred Segal is no different than a lot of fans. When he was an attorney, he would consume sports takes just like anyone else: scrolling Twitter, watching ESPN, and listening to the radio. Mostly, he accepted the bold opinions and predictions for what they were — entertainment. But there was one thing that always got…
fullText:
Fred Segal is no different than a lot of fans. When he was an attorney, he would consume sports takes just like anyone else: scrolling Twitter, watching ESPN, and listening to the radio.

Mostly, he accepted the bold opinions and predictions for what they were — entertainment. But there was one thing that always got under Fred's skin. He hated watching or listening to these pundits pat themselves on the back when one of their bold takes came to fruition.

"I'd see a reporter make a prediction about a team and that team lost, and I'd be like, 'oh, that guy was wrong,'" he told Awful Announcing in an interview. "Then he'd say the same thing the next week about another team, and that team lost, or he'd say something about a player that was going to be great, and then they weren't.

"I'd remember those and then later on that same guy would say something like, 'just like I predicted five days ago, this happened,' and I'd be like, 'Hang on! I can remember three off the top of my head where you were dead wrong. You didn't post those!'"

That is how Freezing Cold Takes was born, and it didn't take long for it to become one of the Twitter feeds every sports fan had to follow.

"I started doing it for fun," Segal said. "Just a troll type thing, maybe."

Those followers wanted to do so much of Segal's research for him, and that troll grew into a real business. Last week, Segal released his second book. Freezing Cold Takes: College Football catalogs plenty of nonsensical opinions and plenty of predictions that turned out to be very, very wrong.

Writing the book was a business opportunity, but it also gave Segal a chance to put some of the best misfires down on paper. That's pretty valuable when your brand was built on the unstable foundations of social media. Plus, it was easy, a pleasure even, for Segal.

Research for the book combined two of his favorite things: reading old newspaper articles and talking about college football. Segal keeps an eye on all sports takes, but as an SEC alum, his radar is always up for college football. It's his favorite sport, and it's the sport that might most consistently give him material.

"The emotion and the passion, nothing beats it," he says. "Everybody takes it so personally. Even in terms of the writers and TV personalities, every game creates a narrative about who is going to the playoff or what coach has to be fired after his second loss."

I asked Segal if he knew who was featured the most in Freezing Cold Takes: College Football. He didn't have the official stats handy, but his guess was either former CBS and Bleacher Report writer Barrett Sallee, OutKick founder Clay Travis, or Yahoo's Dan Wolken.

To be fair to them, though, in 2022, Segal told Dan Patrick that he had to stop tracking Skip Bayless's and Colin Cowherd's missed predictions because they were dominating the Freezing Cold Takes Twitter feed. Had he not made that decision, he may have been able to fill a whole book with just misfires from those two men.

Social media is a tricky thing now. Gauging what value your idea would have in a different environment is hard too. Maybe that's why Segal is quick to point out that he probably would have been beaten to the punch when I ask how he thinks Freezing Cold Takes would have fared if he had launched in 2025 instead of 2015.

He does note that maybe niche content isn't as valuable on social media as it used to be.

"Some very basic concepts on Twitter now work. I'll see something and think, 'oh, this is pretty basic,' and then it just blows up. I can't even tell anymore what people like and what they don't with social media."

People that have been in the sports talk game for a long time know Segal's work. Even if some privately hate it, in public, everyone will say that they know it's all in good fun. They may even say they welcome the occasional heat check.

In my years writing about sports media, though, I have had the chance to talk to students in high schools and universities across the South, and I've been shocked by what a lot of them have to say about Freezing Cold Takes.

So many people in the very early days of their careers view being highlighted by Segal's social media channels as a credibility killer. That was never what Segal intended.

"I don't think it really diminishes credibility. If anything, I think that credibility is already diminished the second a fan reads something they don't like," he says, pointing out how easy it is now for fans to find the exact opinion about their team that they want to read and believe.

Hot takes are a vital part of this industry. Sports talk is the entertainment business, after all. The stakes of what Wolken, Travis, Sallee, Cowherd, and Bayless think will happen just aren't that high. Isn't being interesting what matters most? Being right should just be a bonus.

"The ones who take [Freezing Cold Takes] seriously, I've come to realize they believe that they are doing work that's important," Segal says. "Whether it's covering a team or breaking stories, they are doing important stuff, and they work long and hard to do it. Then I come along, pass around one bad thing, and everyone laughs about it."

Segal has built a thriving business for himself, but there's no mission to the work. The community he has created is there for comedy purposes just as much as sports ones. Are you worried about seeing your name or take show up in his Twitter feed? Then you are, to borrow a phrase, hustling backward.

"It doesn't matter, right? Like, nobody's ever been fired for bad predictions ever. I mean, I can't even think of one."

title: Santos FC adds 700,000m² site for new academy training ground
description: Santos FC has taken an important step toward expanding its sports infrastructure by acquiring a plot of land of approximately 700,000 square meters in São Vicente, intended for the development of the...
fullText:
Santos FC has taken an important step toward expanding its sports infrastructure by acquiring a plot of land of approximately 700,000 square meters in São Vicente, intended for the development of the new Youth Academy Training Center. The acquisition was made possible through an agreement signed with Saint-Gobain, a long-standing commercial partner of the Club, in exchange for commercial and advertising properties.

The negotiation was supported by the City Hall of São Vicente to complete the operation, reinforcing joint efforts in favor of the municipality's development.

"First of all, it is essential to highlight the asset-related importance of this transaction with Saint-Gobain for Santos. It is an area of around 700,000 square meters, and its acquisition represents an important step for the project of the new youth academy training center. Certainly, in the future, we will use this area to expand and modernize the Club's sports infrastructure. Undeniably, this is a milestone for the current management and for Santos FC," said president Marcelo Teixeira.

"We have a historic relationship with Santos and see this agreement as another step in that journey. We believe in the transformative role of sport in society and are confident that this partnership will contribute to the club's future projects. For Saint-Gobain, this is another step in strengthening a relationship that has remained solid over the years," commented Gustavo Siqueira, Vice President of HR and Public Affairs for Saint-Gobain in Latin America.

"It is a great joy to see this transaction succeed. First, because São Vicente is undergoing strong development, especially the Continental Area, where 150,000 people live and which will receive the VLT in the coming years, creating a major development corridor. Second, because Santos Futebol Clube is a global brand, the club where King Pelé played, where Prince Neymar plays, and which will now have the opportunity to see its future and its talents develop on the lands of Brazil's First City. The City Hall of São Vicente, anticipating the legal and environmental issues necessary for the use of the area, after talks with CETESB, requested that the EIA-RIMA be commissioned. This request was granted and will allow projects to be developed in the region while respecting the environment and ensuring the proper use of the area by the club," declared the mayor of São Vicente, Kayo Amado.

The next steps related to the development of the new sports complex include carrying out the applicable environmental studies and procedures, including the process before CETESB and obtaining the necessary licenses and authorizations.

To make the construction of the new training center feasible, Santos FC is working on structuring a specific investment fund to finance the implementation of the project. The model is under development and will be presented after the project's technical consolidation.

title: Drought leaves sports clubs 'praying for rain'
description: Some grass pitches are dry and hard and clubs are struggling to water their playing surfaces.
fullText:
Periods of drought and prolonged hot, dry weather has had a major effect on sports clubs across south-west England, who are feeling the strain.

The unprecedented weather has left some grass pitches extremely dry and hard for clubs with little to no irrigation, with many dependent on meaningful rainfall for recovery.

A hosepipe ban was put in force on 9 August across Devon, Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly as the conditions put "significant pressure" on the regions water supplies.

South West Water said sports pitches and surfaces were "exempt from hosepipe bans where watering is necessary", so long as it took place outside peak hours of 08:00-10:00 BST and 17:00-21:00 BST.

Bill Martin, chairman and assistant groundsman at Plymouth Cricket Club, said he had "never seen the pitch so dry".

He said this summer has been particularly difficult as a groundsman because "it had been a summer of two halves".

He said the first six weeks it was "very very wet" but since then it had been two months without significant rain.

"We've got one tap and one hose, so the real challenge has been getting water on to the surface, particularly the playing wickets.

He said without water, the ground became very dry and the grass disappeared and turned to dust, which was both difficult to play and dangerous.

"Cricket is a fine weather sport, so we've not had interruptions, we've not lost any games and we've been able to play a lot of cricket in the sunshine which has been great, but in terms of actually looking after the ground and preparing decent pitches to play on, it makes it very hard work."

"Unusually for cricketers we have been praying for rain."

The Rugby Football Union (RFU) announced the start of the community rugby season had been delayed until 21 September because of concerns about player welfare and pitch conditions. While the Football Association issued guidance which said there was "no blanket suspension of football on dry grass pitches" but the priority was to keep "football playing safely".

Lynton Football Club made the decision to postpone their opening fixture of the season.

In a post on social media the club said three players had suffered "serious injuries", with two "undoubtedly" because of the hard surfaces and would not risk any further injuries on a "rock hard almost concrete like pitch".

Nick Rich from Saltash Rugby Football Club said he had "never seen the pitch as parched as it is at the moment".

"It's rock solid out there. If you turned the tables and it was frozen in winter, you would not play a game of rugby on it."

He said the decision to delay the season was a good thing for both rugby and safety but did mean there was a delay in revenue for the club.

Just 15 months ago the club reseeded the pitch at great cost.

He said further reseeding took place earlier this summer and they had "waited for rain so the grass seed would germinate and we haven't had it yet".

"There's been some watering going on but clearly nowhere enough and we've put thousands of gallons on it."

It is a similar story at Ivybridge Bowls Club who have "struggled to keep up" with the amount of watering required during the high temperatures.

Malcolm Johnson, club captain and groundsman, said the club's watering system was small and the green should be watered at least four times a day to keep it growing, but was unable to do that because of the hosepipe restrictions imposed.

"We've got to a point now where we have to leave it as it is and are going to have to start from scratch again in the spring."

A small amount of rain caused a game to be called off on Wednesday because the water was not draining away quickly enough.

Johnson said "the surface is that hard that it is not being absorbed - we would like to spike it, we've got all the machinery to do that but it's just too hard".

title: Rams Land 3 Players on NFL’s Top 10 List
description: The Los Angeles Rams boast not one, not two but three of the NFL's top 10 players. The post Rams Land 3 Players on NFL’s Top 10 List appeared first on LA Sports Report.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Rams are facing monumental expectations this year due to their near-miss last season and stacked roster, so it's no surprise the NFL ranked multiple Rams as being among the best in the league.

That said, the number of top-tier players they have is hard to wrap your head around.

Perhaps the easiest way to describe it is this: Of the top 10 players at any position in football, three of them are Rams. No other team has more than one.

The NFL, when revealing who's in their top 10 ranking, included quarterback Matthew Stafford, the reigning MVP; wide receiver Puka Nacua and defensive end Myles Garrett.

Exactly where they fall in that top 10 hasn't been released — that comes next week — but it's still impressive that the team has multiple players ranked that highly in the first place.

Stafford is one of two QBs on the list, Nacua is one of two wide receivers and Garrett is one of two pass rushers, showing just how stiff the competition is for this type of honor.

With those stars and other key contributors like Davante Adams, Kyren Williams and Trent McDuffie, the Rams and coach Sean McVay have a very real shot at a title this season.

Coincidentally, that championship game, Super Bowl LXI, is at the Rams' house, SoFi Stadium in Inglewood.

And the last time the Rams won the Super Bowl in 2022, that game also was played at SoFi Stadium.

Whether it is a matter of happenstance or something just meant to be, the cards are certainly lining up for a Rams run at the title in 2026.

title: Good Sports: Merced teens leave home to pursue pro soccer dreams
description: Leaving home to follow a dream. That's what both Immanuel Ewing and Jorge Salmeron did at just 13 and 14 years old. The boys signed MLS Next Pro contracts with Crew 2.
fullText:
Leaving home to follow a dream.

"At first, it was hard leaving my family," says Jorge Salmeron.

That's what both Immanuel Ewing and Jorge Salmeron did at just 13 and 14 years old.

"It's super hard, especially the first year," Ewing said.

"Leaving your family behind, your siblings behind, but he's definitely willing to make that sacrifice and work hard for it," says Mariana Rivera, Ewing's mother.

Both Immanuel and Jorge grew up playing soccer in Merced with Albion SC.

To reach their goal of the pros, the two made a sacrifice: leave home and join an MLS developmental academy.

"We see them competing at the highest level," says Albion SC Coach Rafael Valencia. "You see it in the intensity they bring in practice."

The Merced kids found their way to Columbus, Ohio, earning a spot with the Columbus Crew Academy.

Each has made appearances with Crew 2, the last step before becoming a pro.

In the inaugural MLS Next Cup, Immanuel won the MVP award for the U-19 championship.

"It's definitely something I didn't think I would end up getting," he said. "I never thought I would be able to achieve something like that."

Now, both Immanuel and Jorge are making more than just an appearance.

The boys signed MLS Next Pro contracts with Crew 2.

"It's just something you've been wanting for your whole life," Jorge said.

The Crew franchise gains two Valley natives after losing one in July.

Fresno native Max Arfsten was picked by the Crew in the 2023 MLS SuperDraft, won an MLS Cup with the team before being named to the U-S men's national team roster and debuting in the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

Max is on his way to the English Championship side with Middlesbrough FC, passing the reins to Immanuel and Jorge to represent the Valley here in the States.

"All the hard work is finally paying off," Jorge said. "It's just a small step to keep pushing forward."

"For all the little kids out here, kind of just give them something to look up to," Immanuel said. "Show them that there's stuff outside of Merced. It's not just this small town. You can do whatever you put your mind to."

title: Bill Rasmussen Had A Crazy Idea. It Became ESPN
description: Bill Rasmussen turned an improbable idea into ESPN, reshaping sports television and leaving a legacy that endured long after he lost control of the network he founded.
fullText:
In August 1978, Bill Rasmussen was stuck in traffic on Interstate 84 with his son, Scott, trying to solve a problem: They had plans for a sports cable network and enough satellite capacity to cover 8,760 hours a year. What could possibly fill all that time?

Scott offered an answer that sounded almost absurd: play sports all day.

From that traffic jam emerged the blueprint for what became the Entertainment and Sports Programming Network, soon known by its initialism, ESPN.

That brainstorm established Rasmussen, who died Aug. 18 at 93 from the effects of Parkinson's disease, as a founding father of around-the-clock sports television and helped change how generations of fans consumed sports.

"He had an idea, and he had a dream," Bob Rauscher, who launched NFL GameDay in 1985, said. "And he made it happen."

Rasmussen's broadcasting career began in western Massachusetts in the 1960s, before he became communications director for the New England Whalers of the World Hockey Association. After being fired alongside the entire Whalers front office in 1978, Rasmussen began exploring the possibility of creating a cable sports operation of his own.

His original concept was a local Connecticut cable channel that could carry University of Connecticut basketball games, following the model of MSG in New York and WGN in Chicago, according to Vince Doria, ESPN's now-retired vice president for news.

Rasmussen was reminded that once the signal was sent to the satellite, it could be received well beyond Connecticut. That realization expanded the possibilities dramatically, Doria said, even though not everyone saw the idea's merit.

"Everybody thought it was a nuts idea at the time," Doria said

Rasmussen had already incorporated E.S.P. Network when the idea crystallized during that August 1978 road trip, he recalled in a 2012 Forbes interview.

"Scott finally said something like, 'Play football all day, for all I care,' and suddenly, the ideas started coming fast and furious during that car ride," Rasmussen recalled in that interview. "We came up with the idea for 'Sports Center,' we had designed the entire building we would be in, we had decided what types of sports we should go after.

"That car ride was where we hung the heavy steel work for the network."

The Entertainment and Sports Programming Network set up shop on land Rasmussen bought in Bristol, Connecticut, and launched with its opening show, SportsCenter, at 7 p.m. on Sept. 7, 1979, available in about 1.4 million cable households.

Rauscher said the concept of a channel devoted to sports highlights and coverage far beyond the three-minute local news segment was unprecedented, making it a "sports fan's dream."

"I think [Rasmussen] understood that there was this appetite there," Rauscher, who came to ESPN in August 1980, said. "There would be this allegiance and loyalty to want to consume that much material."

It also came with challenges. Few people had cable when the network launched and many that did were confused by the network's name, Doria said. Securing enough programming was another challenge, forcing ESPN to fill portions of its schedule with Australian rules football and even circus events.

Rasmussen also had to persuade a trio of constituencies that didn't yet know they needed round-the-clock sports on television: investors to finance it, sports organizations to provide games and advertisers to believe somebody would watch.

Rasmussen parlayed his own $9,000 credit-card advance and $75,000 in financing arranged through K.S. Sweet into the fledgling venture. Stuart Evey, who oversaw who oversaw Getty Oil's investments outside its core oil business, persuaded the company's board to invest $10 million for an 85% stake. Anheuser-Busch signed on as an advertiser with what was then the largest single advertising buy in cable history.

"Bill was the one that sought the financing," Doria said. "He was the one that chased the NCAA. He got the property in Bristol. He made the deal with RCA.

Taking Getty's money, however, also meant surrendering control.

As ESPN prepared to launch, Evey decided to bring on more experienced television management in the form of Chet Simmons, president of NBC Sports. Simmons became ESPN president in July 1979. Rasmussen was moved to chairman, effectively stripping him of day-to-day authority.

Rasmussen left his active role at ESPN in 1980 and remained largely disconnected from the company until then-president George Bodenheimer welcomed him back for ESPN's 20th anniversary in 1999.

"He was gone so quickly," Doria said. "He wasn't there for the heyday of when it really became successful and a household name.

"But without his initiative, perseverance and determination, it doesn't happen. "

Steve Anderson was trying to follow his Pulitzer Prize-winning father, Dave Anderson, into the sports media game when he read about a little cable company in Connecticut that was "hiring anybody."

"I never thought this thing was going to make it," Anderson said. "I was only hoping that it was going to last long enough so I could get some experience and go back to New York, and get a real job at a real network."

ESPN instead became Anderson's professional home for more than three decades, and he credits Rasmussen with helping establish the family culture that defined its early years.

"Many of us who were there back in the '80s and '90s, we talk about the bond that we all had, the camaraderie we all have just being a part of that team," he said, "because we weren't sure ESPN was going to make it."

Rasmussen remained an entrepreneur after leaving ESPN, and advised the Big Ten on television strategy and pursuing several early internet sports ventures. He also spent decades telling the story of ESPN's unlikely creation through speeches and books, culminating in the 2026 documentary and book Sports Heaven: The Birth of ESPN.

He learned he had Parkinson's disease in 2014 and publicly revealed the diagnosis in 2019. He later became an ambassador for the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research and joined its Patient Council.

Even as his health declined and he used a wheelchair, Rasmussen continued gathering in Florida with retired ESPN veterans.

"He always made you feel like he knew you and appreciated what you did for ESPN and everything else," said Anderson. "He was remarkable in that way."

There was, however, a bittersweet element to Rasmussen's relationship with the company he created. He was pushed aside so early that he missed being part of ESPN's emergence as a sports-media powerhouse, Anderson said.

"He never even experienced the early successes of ESPN," he said. "As I got to know him a little bit and got to see him and listen to him talk, I always felt sad for him that he never really experienced the real success of ESPN firsthand."

Yet Anderson said Rasmussen eventually received the respect such an accomplishment deserved. When he attended ESPN alumni gatherings later in life, he was routinely approached by people seeking to express their gratitude.

"Everybody who had been there at ESPN was going up to him thanking him," Anderson said. "Because he was such a humble man and such a nice man, it was easy for everybody to do."

title: Former UFC fighter Shore turns hand to promoting
description: Former UFC fighter Jack Shore turns to combat sports promoting with the first Stand and Bang show in Ebbw Vale,
fullText:
Nearly two years after retiring from fighting in professional mixed martial arts, Jack Shore's name is back on a combat sports poster.

The former UFC fighter from Abertillery remained in the sport as a coach but now turns his hand to fight promotion.

The first iteration of Shore's new Stand and Bang venture is on Saturday, 22 August when 23 bouts will take place inside a 20-foot boxing ring.

It will feature only striking, with no takedowns or grappling, at Ebbw Vale Leisure Centre.

Shore is hoping to make the show a success with the Welsh MMA scene at "an all-time high".

He told BBC Sport Wales: "It was always going to be hard to jump into an MMA or pure Thai show.

"I thought, 'what's a little niche in the market that I can kind of go after?'

"I'm a big fan of ONE Championship and I don't always know the guys fighting but I'll always put it on because it's exciting."

Shore says his event is shaped by friends coming to shows when he was fighting.

He said: "All my mates used to say that if I wasn't fighting, they wouldn't come because they didn't understand the grappling and it was a bit boring.

"To the untrained eye it is, what's more fan friendly than essentially an MMA fight but with no grappling and no wrestling?

"That's what we're trying to do, stand-up fights. Most of them are going to be in MMA gloves so it should make for an entertaining night."

Shore hopes the points scoring makes it easier for the public to follow who is ahead.

He said: "If one guy is inflicting more damage, the average Joe can look at that and say, 'well, that guy's winning'.

"Don't get me wrong, ring control scores and good defence scores. I daresay a flashy move will score a little bit higher than maybe a jab.

"But ultimately the judges are being told that we're scoring on damage."

Jones' career gamble pays off with second UFC run

Shore has been "riding the wave" since the fight night was announced in March and has aimed to put on a fighter-friendly show.

He said: "I know what it's like coming up as an amateur or as a new pro and to have promoters think they're better than you and almost look at you just as if you're funding their pocket.

"As much as I'm running this show to help make a bit of a living, I also want to put the fighters first.

"If I've got to sacrifice a bit of money to make sure this guy is well looked after or make this guy get a fight on short notice, then I've always been more than prepared to do so.

"Being a fighter who has gone into promotion is a big thing because you know what it's like to be on the other side of the coin."

It has been a steep learning curve for Shore, who has had to rebook fights after late withdrawals.

"In my eyes, it's already a success because we've got to the fight week," he said.

"The fact the show is going to go ahead, and I can say that I've promoted my own show, is brilliant.

"It's not even about breaking even or making money or losing money. A success for me will be to just put on a show that the crowd enjoys.

"If it is a success, I promise to just get bigger and better every time."

Shore's retirement at 29 may have come as a shock, having risen up the ranks to the top 15 of the UFC's bantamweight division before swapping to featherweight.

It could be argued that the man affectionately known as 'Tank' still has 

He finished with a professional record of 17 wins and three losses but the 31-year-old is happy in retirement, despite the occasional temptation.

"I'm in the gym every day with the boys and I do like the sparring," said Shore.

"I'm still young enough to compete with the lads and a lot of my coaching style is sparring with them.

"I'm still competing with the top lads in the gym comfortably, and that's not a knock on anyone.

"It's not like I'm a 45-year-old man and I've been retired for two years.

"I'll spar on a Wednesday night and I'll wake up Thursday morning and think that the last thing I want to do now is go to the gym."

Shore says he has had offers since retiring but none of them have persuaded him back.

"My missus is my main influence if I want advice on something. I usually go to her first, then I'll go to my dad.

"She tells me that if I am going to do it, go back and do it properly in the UFC.

"The reality is that I don't want to do that. I'm not going to go and do some circus show just to feed my ego.

"Mentally, I've checked out, even though now and then the demons are creeping. Never say never, I suppose, let's push it to 99% [retired].

title: Why the Pacers picked streaming service DAZN as regional broadcast partner
description: The Pacers announced on Thursday morning that they will be partnering with DAZN, a global sports streaming service based in London, as its TV partner.
fullText:
The Pacers' regional sports television rights have been in some form of limbo for more than three years since one broadcast partner went bankrupt and then the company that emerged in its place quickly found itself unable to make its rights payments.

So this offseason, after Main Street Sports Group -- the owner of the FanDuel Sports Network -- announced that it was winding down operations, the Pacers embarked on a search for a new regional broadcast partner and landed on one that takes a much different approach than the old model. This one does not have a traditional broadcast or cable channel and markets directly to the consumer, but it comes at a price.

The Pacers announced Thursday morning that they have entered into an agreement with the United Kingdom-based sports streaming company DAZN (pronounced Da-Zone) as its exclusive regional broadcast partner. Pacers fans who want to watch games on DAZN would have to download the company's streaming app, which could be done on any internet-connected devices including smart phones, laptops and smart televisions, but DAZN does not have a presence on any cable or satellite packages. The team announced that there will be 22 regular season games available for free on the DAZN app and that 15 of those games would also be expected to available on a local over-the-air broadcast partner. A local partner has not yet been chosen but Pacers executives say they expect to make that choice sometime in the next few weeks before the season starts.

Access to the rest of the games would require a season pass. Full price for the pass is $119.99 for the season, but fans who sign up before Oct. 15 can purchase an early-bird season pass for $59.99. A monthly pass will also be available for $19.99 per month. Season ticket holders will receive a free season pass. There will be a landing page on the DAZN app that will house all of Pacers content where fans will be directed to for subscription.

The Pacers will be in charge of the actual production of the broadcasts, meaning the announcers will remain the same. Chris Denari will be the play-by-play announcer for the 21st consecutive season, Quinn Buckner will be the color analyst, Jeremiah Johnson will be the sideline reporter and Eddie Gill will assist Johnson on the pregame, halftime and postgame shows while also maintaining his role as radio color analyst with Mark Boyle on play-by-play.

Pacers Sports and Entertainment CEO Mel Raines told reporters in an embargoed briefing Wednesday that the contract is a five-year deal, and though it gives the Pacers the opportunity to opt out in the future if the NBA puts together a regional sports television hub as it has been exploring, they could maintain the deal if the NBA and DAZN partner together on the hub, which is a possibility.

DAZN will be partnering with several of the 13 NBA teams whose rights became available when Main Street Sports Group effectively went under. The company already announced a partnership with the Minnesota Timberwolves and Raines indicated there will be more to come.

"When we were looking at partners -- and I should say, we probably talked to a dozen different options across the board -- one of the things we wanted to do was find somebody who we thought could be what the league refers to as their aggregated solution where you would aggregate all the teams," Raines said. "DAZN is certainly a top potential partner and that's been in the news. They were the only partner we were talking to who was going to potentially continue on. We are looking at this as a long-term partnership. It's a five-year deal, but ... the league required all the teams to have a potential out if there was an aggregated solution. We also don't have to necessarily opt into that. We're looking at this as we are happily in a five-year marriage with DAZN and hope the fans jump on board and love the service as much as we do."

Raines and Pacers Sports and Entertainment executive vice president and chief commercial officer Joey Graziano, who also met with the media Wednesday, said they tried to keep fans first and foremost in their thoughts when they were making their decision. They noted, however, that it's harder to please the entire fanbase now that sports and entertainment consumption have become so fragmented.

Graziano said that in their preparation, the Pacers learned that in 2010, almost 88% of households in the Pacers' designated market area had access to paid -- i.e. cable and satellite-- television. In 2026, that number has fallen to around 30%. The consistent trend of cord-cutting is a big reason why Diamond Sports Group -- which operated the Bally Sports Networks -- filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023 and the Main Street Sports Group that ran the Fan Duel Sports Networks had to effectively go out of business at the end of the 2025-26 NBA season. Graziano said that indicated that the Pacers had to pursue a digital-first strategy and market to fans through the internet rather than traditional linear television.

"We needed a solution that our fans could be able to access," Graziano said. "The way most of us are accessing our lives are via the internet in some way, having something that felt accessible across a variety of different modes and channels. That means your phone. That also may mean the tablet that you have. It may mean your gaming console. It may mean your smart television. We wanted something that would meet our fans exactly where they are as they're traveling in their busy lives."

Of course, not all of the Pacers' fans are in the same place and they know they'll have to deal with a portion of the fanbase that will not be pleased with this move. Their could be older fans without home access to the internet or fans who are already paying for television access who will be displeased to be asked to pay money for another subscription. The best the Pacers can do in that case, they noted, is try to be as accessible as possible in trying to guide those fans toward a new experience.

"Of course we're concerned about it," Graziano said. "We're concerned about all of our fans and we're going to be incredibly responsive to any concerns that come about for that. ... We've got to think about how we make sure those fans are able to We have an entire marketing and digital team who is hyper focused on fan feedback and we will be responsive to fan's concerns about their ability to access. That's an important part of our thought of how do you bring this together. There certainly will be some fans that may represent some challenges and as an organization we will address them."

Raines noted that the Pacers do not have access to some over-the-air opportunities that are available to others. Several teams, including the Bucks, Magic and Heat, have announced that they will broadcast all of their games on free over-the-air television this season. Raines said those teams were able to take advantage of effectively dead channels on their local packages that aren't available in the Indianapolis area.

"Some markets had the opportunity with a Scripps or a Grey to have an empty channel that is already bought into the lower tier of Comcast or Spectrum or DirecTV or Dish," Raines said. "That's not available in our market right now. As you know there's been a lot of consolidation. Unfortunately we didn't have that opportunity."

They also couldn't expect to ask a local broadcast affiliate of one of the big four national networks -- ABC, CBS, NBC and FOX -- to commit to showing all of the games that will not be broadcast nationally. The Pacers will appear on some form of national broadcast 11 times in their 82 regular season games -- once on ESPN, once on NBC, four times on Amazon Prime and five times on Peacock. Even getting 15 games over the air as they plan to, Raines said, is ambitious.

"They can't clear 71 games," Raines said. "They have network programming that they can't pre-empt 71 times. To get 15 at their peak season is difficult to be honest. If it was easy we'd be telling you who it was today. They have to navigate being able to pre-empt broadcast TV. There really isn't a single solution out there that hits 100% of the fans anymore or I'd tell you those 13 teams -- us being one of them -- would have already done that deal six months ago. That's what we're trying to do and I think our best shot at it is a partner like this."

DAZN has extensive experience with this situation, especially overseas, and the company was aggressive in courting the 13 teams that had partnered with Main Street. Raines said DAZN was the only potential partner that wanted to come to Indiana for an in-person meeting. Zander Berlinksi, DAZN's senior vice president of strategy and business development, also attended Wednesday's press briefing.

According to the press release announcing the partnership, DAZN streams more than 140,000 live events annually and is available in more than 200 markets worldwide. The United States overall market accounts for a relatively small percentage of its business, but it partners with some of the biggest sports leagues in Europe and Japan, and also serves as a global distributor for U.S. sports leagues. Berlinski said DAZN owns the exclusive rights to Italy's Serie A soccer league and Spain's La Liga as well as much of the domestic baseball in Japan. It also, according to Berlinski, is the largest partner for the NFL internationally outside of the U.S. and China as it platforms NFL Game Pass internationally.

"Over the last 10 years, we've built a tremendous tech platform that is powered by 2,000-plus engineers that is purpose-built for sports," Berlinski said, "and has experienced working with teams and leagues across the world to help grow audiences."

Dustin Dopirak covers the Pacers all season. Get more coverage on IndyStarTV and with the Pacers Insider newsletter.

title: If You Loved 'The Hawk,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next
description: If you’re a big fan of Will Ferrell’s newest sports comedy, there’s one movie you should watch immediately.
fullText:
No one does sports comedy like Will Ferrell. His loud, crude, and slightly unbalanced (okay, often extremely unbalanced) comedic persona is ideal for a character like Lonnie Hawkins, aka The Hawk, an aging former pro golfer chasing one last bit of glory while hilariously getting in his own way. What’s great about The Hawk is how precisely pitched it is: Ferrell’s brand of chaos contrasts perfectly with the straitlaced, stuffy world of golf, delivering big laughs with a strong emotional core. If you’re looking for more sports-related mayhem, you should immediately go to Apple TV and watch The Dink.

If there’s an actor capable of matching Will Ferrell’s manic energy, it’s Jake Johnson. Though Johnson tends to be a bit more laid back in his approach, he’s one of the few comedians working today who can sell a ridiculous breakdown and a shouty tirade at the same level, and he’s in top form in The Dink. Johnson plays Dusty “The Hammer” Boyd, who was a tennis prodigy as a kid, known for his incredibly precise and powerful serve. When he breaks his wrist during a match with fellow up-and-comer Andy Roddick (yeah, the Andy Roddick), he loses his chance at greatness and the respect of his father, Chuck (Ed Harris in full scowl). As an adult, he’s an instructor at his father’s tennis club, still haunted by his failure and his father’s disappointment.

Dusty is hilarious: Filled with rage, followed around by an obsequious assistant, PJ (Aaron Chen), who stokes his delusions of greatness, and absolutely, positively opposed to pickleball in any form. When club member Skip Pigliani (Patton Oswalt) advocates for an official pickleball court, Chuck agrees to settle the matter with a “tennis duel” per the club’s charter. Dusty wins the chance to represent the club in the duel, but injures his hand, prompting Chuck to replace him. Chuck is advised to play pickleball as rehabilitation, leading him to meet Candace (Mary Steenburgen). Slowly, Dusty realizes how stunted he’s been his whole life—and how much he’s lied to himself about the reasons for his mediocrity.

Along the way, however, we get a lot of Dusty’s very funny outbursts and plenty of over-the-top humor that would make Ferrell proud. The final “duel” is one of the funniest things you’ll see in any pickleball-themed film, including Andy Roddick being recruited by Chuck to play against Dusty, and John McEnroe randomly showing up to eat hot dogs and do a very funny play-by-play of the match. The Dink is funny, but it’s also got a lot of heart, and it has something to say about found family, how competition can sour into obsession, and, yes, pickleball. If you loved The Hawk, it’s the perfect follow-up. Stream The Dink on Apple TV.

Need even more athletic chaos in your movie rotation? Here are a few more movies that absolutely fit the vibe that The Hawk is laying down.

If you love the “snobs versus slobs” thread embedded in The Hawk, go watch this all-time great golf comedy. With a behind-the-scenes production almost as insane as the comedy on the screen, Caddyshack represents a high-water mark for Bill Murray, Chevy Chase, and Rodney Dangerfield (with able support by an absolutely deranged Ted Knight) as they (sometimes literally) chew the scenery at the uber-fancy Bushwood Country Club There’s a story somewhere in there, but mainly this is just a few comedy geniuses having a great time on the golf course, and fans of The Hawk will love it—especially Dangerfield’s loud and proud Al Czervik. Rent Caddyshack on Prime Video.

If you want more golf comedy that dances over the line of absurdity with what scientists call enthusiasm, this Adam Sandler classic is required viewing. Sandler plays the title character, an aspiring hockey player with a powerful slapshot, no other skills, and a serious anger problem. When he needs to make a bucket of money to save his grandmother’s house, he discovers that his slapshot skills translate to an ability to drive a golf ball—and begins hustling golfers for cash. When he’s recruited by former golf star Chubbs Peterson (Carl Weathers) to compete professionally, Happy has to up his game and control his anger—and since this is an Adam Sandler film, you can guess how badly the latter goes. If for no other reason, watch this to witness Sandler and Bob Barker have a ridiculously extended fistfight. Rent Happy Gilmore on Prime Video.

If you came for Will Ferrell’s brand of insanity in The Hawk, you might as well lean in. Talladega Nights: The Ballad of Ricky Bobby is the best of Ferrell’s sports-themed comedies, fusing Ferrell’s trademark absurdity with a surprisingly sophisticated take on professional racing. You can tell everyone involved actually likes NASCAR, and thus knows exactly how to make a little fun of it, and everyone is at the top of their game, from Ferrell to John C. Reilly to Sacha Baron Cohen as Ricky Bobby’s nemesis, the very French Jean Girard. Rent Talladega Nights: The Ballad of Ricky Bobby on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for a golf comedy with a slightly gentler and less-deranged sensibility, check out Tin Cup. Kevin Costner plays Roy McAvoy, a former pro golfer who blew his big chance and now wallows in alcoholic mediocrity. When he meets and falls for Dr. Molly Griswold (Renee Russo), who is dating his former peer David Simms (Don Johnson), Roy decides to take a (very) long shot at getting into the U.S. Open. It’s a different kind of funny, just as golfy, and a slightly more serious take on a similar storyline. Rent Tin Cup on Prime Video.

On the other hand, if you want a more deranged sports comedy, this is it. Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story takes what might be the most despised schoolyard game of all time and generates hilarity. To save his failing gym, Peter LaFleur (Vince Vaughn) and his friends enter a dodgeball competition in Las Vegas, and find themselves playing against Peter’s enemy, rival gym owner White Goodman (a very caffeinated Ben Stiller) and his team of ringers. If you hear the phrase “Rip Torn in a wheelchair throwing wrenches at people” and laugh instinctively, this is the movie for you. Stream Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

title: Sports tech company Rule42 invests in AUSL, acquires Softball America
description: Rule42 — a new sports tech company founded by former Intel president Renée James — is investing in AUSL and has acquired Softball America.
fullText:
As the parent of Major League Baseball prospect, Renée James got a first-hand look at how chaotic, strenuous and inaccessible the scouting process could be for a young athlete aiming to land a college scholarship or a professional contract.

The former president of the Intel Corporation, who then also founded and sold Ampere Computing, thought to herself: "We can do better."

"There's no scouting for women. The men scouting for amateur (sports) is very pay-to-play," James told USA TODAY Sports. "It is such a rough path that I thought, you know, use your power for good, you could make this better for a lot of kids who didn't make it who could have gotten college scholarships."

So, a few weeks ago, James launched Rule42 — a sports technology company aiming to modernize the discovery process for athletes, scouts and teams.

And softball is the sport that Rule42 is jumping into first with both feet.

Rule42 announced on Wednesday, Aug. 18 that it is making a significant investment in the Athletes Unlimited Softball League, which just completed its second full season. Alongside MLB, the Milwaukee Brewers, Ryan Sanders Baseball and Athletes Unlimited, the Rule42 Sports Group will be among the league's largest investors. James will also join the AUSL's Board of Directors.

Additionally, Rule42 has acquired Softball America, one of the leading digital publications that covers all levels of the sport with editorial news and prospect rankings. Softball America's top 150 prospect rankings for the high school class of 2028 debuted on Rule42's website on Tuesday.

Softball America will become "Softball America by Rule42" and the entirety of the digital publication's team will be employed by James' company. Tara Henry, the general manager of Softball America, is also now the Vice President of Softball at Rule42.

"The idea is to make (Rule42) pretty synonymous with what we're doing and just continue to grow the game from the youth market to the college market, all the way to the pro market," Henry told USA TODAY Sports. "Marrying the tech side and the sports side, it was a no-brainer for us. I'm just really excited that we'll be able to give more athletes opportunities beyond the Power Four, beyond the mid-majors, and really find places to develop and grow talent."

Softball America's rankings will be free to access on Rule42's website, while it will still publish subscriber-only editorial content on the On3 network.

Rule42 is self-funded by James and plans to build an AI-powered technology platform that gives athletes an equal shot at being discovered by college and pro scouts. The service will be free to use for athletes and parents.

The genesis for starting Rule42 came from James watching other parents struggle to get their kids noticed as she was seeing her son Ryan become an MLB prospect who was drafted in the third round this year by the Toronto Blue Jays out of the University of Oregon.

And then James discovered that the process is even tougher for women.

"It's more than hard. It's heartbreaking. These parents are taking second mortgages on their homes. For the women, you have to go to a college program to become a pro," James said. "There's no formal scouting. There isn't the infrastructure for women. So, for women, we can leapfrog the decades of the scouting structure that there is for men by using technology.

"And now there are major scholarships for girls that we need to match them with. These coaches in these programs do not have time to find all the talent out there."

What James is referring to was a domino that fell with the landmark House v. NCAA settlement in 2025 which eliminated sport-specific scholarship caps. It more than doubled the possible number of athletic scholarships that can be offered to women at the Division I level. Previously, many softball programs — and other women's college sports teams — didn't have the full complement of scholarships that matched their roster sizes.

With its investment in AUSL, Rule42 will have a footprint at all levels of softball, a sport that has a growing audience.

This year's Women's College World Series smashed viewership records for ESPN as it was the most watched WCWS on record, drawing an average of 1.6 million viewers per game. And for the AUSL, ABC drew an average audience of 732,000 viewers for Game 1 of its championship series this year, making it the most-watched professional softball game on record.

All of that is building toward the sport making its return to the Olympics in 2028 on American soil.

"We're incredibly excited to have Renée on board as an investor," Jon Patricof, CEO of Athletes Unlimited, told USA TODAY Sports. "She is one of the most accomplished, experienced and successful executives in the technology industry. She is someone who is going to offer us so much, and has already offered so much advice and guidance on how to build a large, scalable business."

With Kim Ng as its commissioner, merchandise sales for the AUSL increased by 110% this season and social media impressions grew by 97%. Year-over-year television viewership grew by more than 150% as the AUSL had more than 90 games distributed across ESPN platforms, CBS Sports Network and MLB Network this season.

"It's a very positive opportunity," James said. "There are girls everywhere playing softball and they wonder, what comes next? And now, the answer is they can be a pro too, and that is why I'm investing in AUSL. I want to see us grow. I want to see us continue."

Athletes Unlimited announced last month that it was pausing play in its women's basketball and volleyball leagues. But Patricof made it clear the organization is all-in on softball.

"We've had so much success with softball. We've significantly expanded our footprint over the last two years in that sport," Patricof said. "In basketball and volleyball, our thoughts are we want to up the trajectory of what we're achieving with softball. If we're going to go forward in either of those sports, it's going to be in a big and meaningful way, and so, we're exploring a host of opportunities.

"But for now, softball has become far and away the largest part of the Athletes Unlimited portfolio. We're just coming off an amazing season and we're ready for 2027."

title: Wales sports minister meets WRU after fans' fears
description: Wales' sports minister Heledd Fychan meets with Welsh Rugby Union to express fears of split with fans over three-team plan.
fullText:
Wales' sports minister has met with the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) after concerns of a "disconnect" between the governing body and fans.

The WRU has doubled down in recent weeks on plans to cut a professional men's side, with Scarlets or Ospreys set to be culled by 2028.

Heledd Fychan MS, the Senedd's chief whip and cabinet minister for culture and sport, insisted the WRU is an independent organisation and Welsh government has no direct role in its decision-making.

But in a statement, Fychan said: "Given the importance of rugby to communities across Wales, I met with the WRU last week in my capacity as cabinet minister for culture and sport to discuss the future of professional rugby in Wales.

"I conveyed the concerns raised by supporters and stressed the importance of fully considering the impact of any decisions on clubs, communities and the long-term future of the game across Wales.

"I welcome the WRU's willingness to continue discussions as part of this process. The Welsh government will remain engaged and committed to supporting rugby at all levels across Wales."

WRU condemns abuse and doubles down on three-team plan

WRU confirms Ospreys or Scarlets will be cut

Scarlets vow to remain at heart of west Wales

Fychan went into further detail on meeting with the WRU on the latest edition of BBC Wales' podcast Walescast.

She said it was a good conversation, with WRU chief executive Abi Tierney present.

"I don't think it'd be any surprise that I've received a lot of correspondence from both Scarlets and Ospreys fans," said Fychan.

"It was an opportunity for me to again reiterate the importance of the WRU properly engaging with communities."

Fychan stated the Welsh government did not have an opinion on whether a reduction to three sides was the way forward because the WRU is a private company.

But she added: "I was very clear in terms of this new culture and sports strategy for Wales that the future of rugby as a community game is really important as well as that professional side and that I wanted to see, as part of the proposals that they have, how are they addressing those historic concerns."

Fychan said the WRU gave her some "positive news in terms of what's been happening with women's rugby here in Wales".

"That was positive to hear that especially because of what happened a few years ago and the concerns around that," said Fychan.

"But clearly people in Wales, and especially those Scarlets and Ospreys fans, currently feel they're not being listened to.

"There's that disconnect which is I think a huge concern between the WRU and the communities that they seek to work with.

"So, it was an opportunity to say 'please work with them' because people are concerned about the economic impact of the closure of either club as well."

This is not the first time this year that politicians have commented on the state of Welsh rugby.

In January, the Welsh Affairs Select Committee told the WRU the governing body was out of touch with fans over its aims to cut a professional team.

Former chair Richard Collier-Keywood and Tierney were both quizzed in Westminster on the controversial plans to reduce the number of regional sides to three.

They were told afterwards by going down this path that they risked "throwing the baby out with the bath water and alienating supporters", while the cross-party group said there was "an immense disconnect between the WRU and fans".

In March, politicians in the Senedd stated the WRU had "lost the argument" over the future of the professional game after it appeared before the sport and culture committee.

Committee chair Delyth Jewell said Welsh rugby was in a "perilous state" but urged the governing body to find an alternative approach or risk "losing the soul" of Welsh rugby.

Welsh rugby's ins, outs and re-signings for 2026-27

It is has been another bruising week for the WRU with a concerted attempt to try to oust the board, featuring a plea by former Wales captain Jonathan Davies.

This came after the same calls from businesswoman and former Cardiff board member Hayley Parsons, while former Principality Building Society chief operating officer Rob Regan has offered to oversee an interim board.

The WRU board released a statement on Saturday and, while it did not directly address calls for its members to resign, it stated that "personal insults and attacks that have become far too commonplace are unacceptable".

title: Bezos consortium bought nearly 40 percent of Liverpool: report
description: A consortium including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos bought close to 40 percent of Premier League giants Liverpool, the Athletic reported Tuesday.It was initially reported that 1892 Holdings had purchased a third of the club from Fenway Sports Group, the owners of 20-time English champions Liverpool, but the Athletic said the actual figure was closer to 38 percent.
fullText:
A consortium including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos bought close to 40 percent of Premier League giants Liverpool, the Athletic reported Tuesday.

It was initially reported that 1892 Holdings had purchased a third of the club from Fenway Sports Group, the owners of 20-time English champions Liverpool, but the Athletic said the actual figure was closer to 38 percent.

There is also an option for the consortium to buy a controlling stake in Liverpool in the next 12 months, though that does not involve a formal commitment.

US-based FSG said Friday it had agreed the deal with 1892 Holdings, a consortium led by British-Indian millionaire Amit Bhatia and also featuring Bezos and Eduardo Saverin, who co-founded Facebook.

American tycoon Bezos is the fourth-richest person in the world, with an estimated net worth of $256 billion.

This is Bezos's first investment in a sports team after he was previously linked with purchasing NFL franchises Seattle Seahawks and Washington Commanders.

Bhatia, the son-in-law of Indian billionaire Lakshmi Mittal, was QPR co-owner for 18 years before stepping away from the English Championship club once his Liverpool link became public knowledge.

FSG bought Liverpool for £300 million ($406 million) in 2010 and sold a minority stake of around three percent to global sports investment firm Dynasty Equity three years ago.

Liverpool start their Premier League campaign at Newcastle on Sunday.

They are looking to bounce back from a disappointing fifth-place finish in the top flight last season.

That failure led to Arne Slot being sacked as Liverpool manager just 12 months after he masterminded a Premier League title triumph in his first season since succeeding Jurgen Klopp.

With several weeks until the Premier League transfer window closes, the new investment could be a boost to Reds boss Andoni Iraola as he looks to strengthen his squad for the new season.

Liverpool have so far spent around £94 million on signing Jeremy Jacquet and Victor Munoz since the end of last term.

title: 4-Time World Champion Surfer Llywelyn Williams Says Losing His Leg Led to Successful Sports Career: ‘I Was Born Again’
description: While skateboarding when he was 16 years old, Williams was hit by a car, which led to a leg amputation
fullText:
Llywelyn Williams had his leg amputated when he was 16 after a car hit him while he was skateboarding

Since then, the professional para surfer has won four ISA World Championships and dozens of other medals around the world

"Disability for me has elevated my life — anything is possible if you have any kind of disability," the U.K. athlete said

David Williams remembers 2011, when his teen son, Llywelyn Williams, was "nearly dead" after a car hit the then-teenager while he was skateboarding.

Llywelyn, who was 16 at the time, suffered severe injuries — a shattered pelvis, split liver, dislocated hips and collapsed lungs — as well as the loss of his right leg above the knee, Llywelyn shared in a recap of his life and career.

Recalling his surfer son's life-changing moment, David said in the BBC documentary Our Lives: Beyond the Waves, "To think he was nearly dead on the side of the road when the accident happened ... to being the world champion. Once he got his first wave back, there was no stopping him."

Llywelyn, now in his early 30s, has four adaptive surfing world championship titles to his name.

The U.K. athlete told the BBC he felt like he was "born again" when he "got back in the ocean" after his leg was amputated.

"From the moment I woke up in the hospital, my goal was clear — I was going to surf again and come back stronger than ever," Llywelyn wrote in his recap. "As I emerged from my coma, I told my friend Will that I was determined to return to the water and surf better than before."

He added, "My hospital room became my motivation, decorated with images of waves, surf culture and the familiar scent of Sex Wax air fresheners, making it the best-smelling room in the hospital."

In the BBC doc, Llywelyn's mom, Eirian Parry, recalled the "beautiful moment" that her son's friends carried him into the water after the amputation.

Nearly 15 years after the car accident, the professional para surfer has since won four ISA World Championships and earned more than 50 medals at other competitions around the world.

Most recently, Llywelyn won the Bright Sky Australian Pro Adaptive Surfing Championship as the kneeling champion in March, and he finished third at the North Shore Prosthetics Hawaiian Surfing Championships in May.

"Disability for me has elevated my life — anything is possible if you have any kind of disability," the surfer told the BBC.

Watch live coverage of both finals on BBC Two and iPlayer and listen to ball-by-ball commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra and BBC Sounds. TV and radio coverage alongside live text and in-play video highlights on the BBC Sport website and app.

Despite Manchester City's Women's Super League win, it's Arsenal who would come out on top in a combined 2025-26 Premier League and WSL table.

A formidable strikeforce of Erling Haaland and Khadija Shaw is a scary thought though - the pair netted a combined total of 48 league goals last season.

England's flawless record in the women's Six Nations is only enough for second in the combined table due to just a single win in the men's competition.

We have to merge the points from two different golf competitions across two years to get a picture of how a combined European side would fare against a combined USA team.

Europe's two-point victory in the 2025 Ryder Cup isn't enough to get them over the line, with the US just edging it thanks to their three-point win in the Solheim Cup in 2024.

title: 6 NBA teams screwed over by the schedule release
description: The idea of playing a balanced schedule is a rarity in American professional sports. An NFL team that finishes in first place in their division one year draws other first-place teams on the schedule the next year. NHL calendars lean heavily on divisional matchups and regional rivalries. MLB moved to a more balanced schedule in […]
fullText:
The idea of playing a balanced schedule is a rarity in American professional sports. An NFL team that finishes in first place in their division one year draws other first-place teams on the schedule the next year. NHL calendars lean heavily on divisional matchups and regional rivalries. MLB moved to a more balanced schedule in 2023, reducing the number of division games and increasing interleague play to even things out.

The NBA does not play a balanced schedule, but the biggest factor in an individual team's success often feels like it has more to do with the travel arrangements than who they're playing on a particular night. Trimming the NBA's 82-game regular season schedule always felt like a silver bullet for many of the league's most pressing problems. Until that happens, teams are still jetting around the country every night to try to sell out as many arenas as possible.

The 2026-27 NBA schedule came out this week. Read our take on the league's 10 biggest rivalries for the upcoming season. With a little help from Shamit Dua's NBA Schedule Dash Board, these are the teams who got hit the hardest by the schedule makers this year.

The Celtics' 16 back-to-backs are in a five-way tie for the most in the NBA. They play 22 times in a stretch of three games in four nights, which ranks as the eighth hardest in the league. They are -4 in "net rest" games, which measures who the more tired opponent is in a given game. The Celtics aren't just dealing with the loss of Jaylen Brown this season, they're also needing to navigate one of the league's hardest travel schedules. I still think the Celtics will be a regular season wins machine, and I wouldn't count them out for grabbing the No. 1 seed in the East, but the road to get there looks more daunting after the schedule release.

The Pelicans have the hardest schedule in the NBA this year. New Orleans plays a league-leading 16 back-to-backs, they're the only team in the NBA with 27 'three in four nights' stretches, and they have a -5 net rest disadvantage. The Pelicans already had the league's seventh-lowest over/under at 29.5 wins coming into the season, and it feels like it's going to be an uphill climb to even hit that number. New head coach Jamahl Mosley has his work cut out for him. After years of believing in Zion Williamson, I'm finally giving up the dream that he can be one of the NBA's best players. At this point, I'm more interested in seeing what Jeremiah Fears and Derik Queen can do together.

The Bulls are one of the league-leaders with 15 back-to-backs this season. They play a stretch of three games in four nights 24 times, which is the fourth most in the league. They're -3 on "net rest," which is third-hardest in the league. The Bulls also have five time zone crossings on no rest, which is the fifth-most in the league. The first 15 games of the season are especially brutal for Chicago, with two games against Boston, two games against the Knicks, two games against the Sixers, and one game each vs. San Antonio, Minnesota, and Cleveland. The Bulls are starting yet another rebuild, but it's going to be difficult for this fanbase to be patient when the team has the third worst cumulative record in the NBA after the last nine seasons. This year is more about figuring out if they have a future star in Caleb Wilson, and seeing how Matas Buzelis and Josh Giddey develop in their third year together. The Bulls actually have a decent bench led by Leonard Miller, Jalen Smith, and Tre Jones, and they're going to need it with this type of schedule.

The Cavs missed out on LeBron James and got a tough schedule to boot. Cleveland is tied for the league-lead with 16 back-to-backs. They have 23 'three in four nights' games, which is the sixth hardest in the NBA. They're a -2 in rest advantage, also sixth hardest. The Cavs have done a whole lot of nothing this summer coming off the world's least convincing conference finals run, but there's still time to potentially land Peyton Watson or swing a big trade. I just get the sense that Cleveland's Eastern Conference rivals are passing them by … unless Evan Mobley has another leap left in him.

The Mavericks have 16 back-to-backs (tied for the most in the league), and they're at a -3 net rest advantage. It will be fascinating to see how Dallas manages Kyrie Irving as he returns from a torn ACL at age-34. The team will also have to manage Dereck Lively II, because the 22-year-old big man still hasn't been cleared to run after having foot surgery in December. I could see a world where Cooper Flagg takes a big leap and carries the Mavs to playoff contention, but it's important to remember Flagg won't turn 20 years old until just before Christmas. It might be wise for Dallas' new front office to take a more long-term view around their franchise star.

The Lakers play 15 back-to-backs. They face three games in four nights 26 times, which is the second most in the league. There's so much riding on Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves this year. Both of them dealt with injuries last year, playing 115 out of a possible 164 games. That's not going to cut it this year. Doncic and Reaves need to carry this offense every night without LeBron James around, and the Lakers probably don't want to know what happens when Quentin Grimes needs to be their first or second option for a night. Will the Lakers have a plan to save Luka in some back-to-backs? It's going to be a battle in the Western Conference every night, but the Lakers really just need him healthy for the playoffs, unlike last year.

title: Good Sports: Fresno dad turns hobby into unforgettable moment with Dallas Cowboys QB Dak Prescott
description: A Fresno father's custom tribute hat for Dak Prescott turned a year-old painting hobby into an unforgettable, full-circle moment.
fullText:
A Fresno father's painting hobby led to an unforgettable encounter when Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott not only accepted one of his custom hats, but later wore it and sought out the artist behind it.

Mario Corona, a stay-at-home dad, licensed EMT and aspiring firefighter, began painting hats about a year ago. He said he never expected one of his designs would end up in the hands of an NFL quarterback.

"A day that I definitely won't forget," Corona said.

Recently, Corona completed a Dallas Cowboys collection that included a tribute to Prescott's brother, Jace. Prescott lost his brother to suicide in 2020 and has spoken publicly about raising awareness since then.

Corona created what he calls an "Angel Hat," featuring a portrait of Jace on the side.

"I know as a Cowboys fan, as a Dak fan, I know how much his brother meant to him and his motivation," Corona said.

Corona traveled to Cowboys training camp in Oxnard hoping to personally give the hat to Prescott. During First Responders Appreciation Day, he was able to get on the field.

"The players right in front of Dak were CeeDee [Lamb] and [George] Pickens, which were the players that were on my hat that I was wearing at the time. So I got caught up in trying to show them the hat I was wearing," Corona said. "By the time they passed and I turned back, Dak was already right here. I just babbled out whatever words were trying to come out of my mouth. Luckily, he did grab it before walking off."

Prescott accepted the hat without initially noticing the portrait painted on its side.

"I was happy that I knew he took it at least. I was actually leaving training camp pretty bummed. I didn't sell any hats, I didn't get any autographs," Corona said.

After leaving camp, Corona saw photos on social media showing Prescott wearing the hat. That is when he learned the quarterback was looking for the artist who created it.

"Got in the car, drove back... they're like, dude, you're going to have to go to the hotel," Corona said.

Corona later reunited with Prescott and captured the interaction on his Meta glasses.

"It was just real. It felt real," Corona said. "You know that moment was bigger than an autograph."

Throughout the remainder of training camp, Prescott was seen wearing Corona's hat.

The positive response to his work has encouraged Corona to take the next step with his business. He said he plans to open for commissions in November.

"As long as you're passionate about it and you stay dedicated... progress will come. If you're trying, you're going to have improvement. It for sure has paid off," Corona said.

title: Fact Check: FAKE Sports Journalist 'Marc Jacobs' Falsely Reported Russell Westbrook Was Signing With Hapoel Tel Aviv in Israel
description: Did a real sports journalist named "Marc Jacobs" report that Russell Westbrook was signing with Hapoel Tel Aviv in Israel? No, that's not true: There was no evidence that Westbrook, a 37-year-old NBA free agent, had signed with the Israeli...
fullText:
Did a real sports journalist named "Marc Jacobs" report that Russell Westbrook was signing with Hapoel Tel Aviv in Israel? No, that's not true: There was no evidence that Westbrook, a 37-year-old NBA free agent, had signed with the Israeli professional team as of Aug. 12, 2026. The claim came from a fake sports reporter on a parody account, citing a story that does not exist.

The claim appeared in a post and image (archived here) by the @MJacobsLF account on X on Aug. 9, 2026. It read:

REPORT: Russell #Westbrook and Hapoel Tel Aviv reportedly have mutual interest, with talks between the two sides continuing to expand. The former MVP is seriously considering a move overseas this season. Per @TheAthletic

A deal would mark the first time Westbrook plays professionally outside the NBA.

This is what the post looked like on X at the time of writing:

The Marc Jacobs X profile describes the persona as a "Senior NBA Writer & Reporter for @LakerFilm." Jacobs is not a mainstream, credentialed journalist and has fewer than 4,300 followers as of Aug. 12, 2026. The @LakerFilm account (archived here) had fewer than 40 followers as of Aug. 12, 2026, and had the display name "FOLLOW MJacobsLF."

Lead Stories searched Google News (archived here) and Yahoo News (archived here) and did not find any matching reports from credible news outlets reporting that Westbrook was in talks with Hapoel Tel Aviv. The searches used the terms "Russell Westbrook," "Hapoel Tel Aviv," and "Marc Jacobs."

However, several publications picked up the claim as legitimate reporting, including the Jerusalem Post (archived here), which later removed the story (archived here) from its website.

The post on X also falsely cited The Athletic (@TheAthletic) to substantiate its claim about Westbrook. The Athletic, owned by The New York Times Company, did not report the story (archived here). A Google Advanced Search of the site (archived here) by Lead Stories produced the same results.
